title: Streaming SSE chunking/backpressure debug notes (repro + commands)
content:
Context:
Quick personal notes while chasing an intermittent streaming bug where SSE / text/event-stream responses either: (a) stall mid-stream for clients (long pause >10s between events), (b) arrive as a single large chunk at the client (no incremental updates), or (c) cause server memory growth until the connection terminates. Behavior mostly seen behind our staging HTTP proxy (nginx) and reproduces sometimes with curl/node-fetch but not with a raw tcp client.

Observed symptoms:
- curl -N shows nothing for 8-20s then a burst of multiple events.
- Browser Fetch-based client receives a single large payload after a delay.
- Node server logs: no errors but heap grows when many concurrent streams are open.
- Nginx access log shows steady 200 with long request durations; error log occasionally: "upstream prematurely closed connection".

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Proxy/nginx buffering is aggregating chunked data before flushing to client (proxy_buffering on).
2) TLS/ALB or ingress is buffering until connection hits some threshold (ALB does TLS termination + buffering).
3) Runtime not calling flush() / not using WriteHeader/Flush correctly (Go) which prevents kernel-level flush.
4) gzip/compression middleware wraps and buffers, causing delayed output.
5) HTTP/2 multiplexing differences: http2 may buffer differently; client using http1 vs http2 changes behavior.
6) Long GC pauses on server under high concurrency contributing to gaps.

Repro notes and commands (useful quick commands to reproduce locally / stage):
1) Minimal repro server (Go) that streams SSE every 1s:

  # go-sse-repro.go (quick run)
  package main
  import (
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "time"
  )
  func handler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
    w.Header().Set("Cache-Control", "no-cache")
    w.WriteHeader(200)
    flusher, _ := w.(http.Flusher)
    for i := 0; i < 20; i++ {
      fmt.Fprintf(w, "data: event %d\n\n", i)
      flusher.Flush() // critical
      time.Sleep(1 * time.Second)
    }
  }
  func main() {
    http.HandleFunc("/sse", handler)
    http.ListenAndServe(":8083", nil)
  }

Run: go run go-sse-repro.go  (then curl below)

2) Simple curl tests:
  # HTTP/1.1, no buffering at client:
  curl -i -N --http1.1 http://localhost:8083/sse

  # Force HTTP/2 (if server supports)
  curl -i -N --http2 http://localhost:8083/sse

3) Test through nginx (local nginx conf snippet used for repro):
  # nginx.conf snippet used during debugging:
  server {
    listen 8080;
    location /sse/ {
      proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8083/sse;
      proxy_http_version 1.1;
      proxy_set_header Connection ""; # ensure keepalive works
      proxy_buffering off;        # MUST be off for streaming
      proxy_cache off;
      chunked_transfer_encoding on;
    }
  }

  # Test via nginx:
  curl -i -N http://localhost:8080/sse/

Observed: when proxy_buffering was left default (on), curl via nginx got first event immediately then nothing, then a burst. Turning proxy_buffering off reduced the bursts but didn't eliminate pauses entirely.

4) Confirm ALB / LB buffering: repro against staging ALB and compare headers:
  # curl to staging (show intermediate headers)
  curl -i -N -v https://staging-api.redwood-inference.com/sse/ 2>&1 | tee curl-staging.log

Look for: 'X-Accel-Buffering' or 'transfer-encoding: chunked' and whether any proxy adds buffering headers. Also check Cloudfront/ALB docs about streaming and idle timeouts.

5) Client repro (node):
  // node-stream-client.js
  const fetch = require('node-fetch')
  (async () => {
    const res = await fetch('http://localhost:8080/sse/', {headers: {'Accept': 'text/event-stream'}})
    console.log('status', res.status)
    const reader = res.body.getReader() // node 18+
    while(true) {
      const {done, value} = await reader.read()
      if(done) break
      console.log('chunk len', value.length)
      // print chunk as string
      console.log(new TextDecoder().decode(value))
    }
  })()

Note: node's stream API shows long periods with no bytes read, then many bytes in one chunk when buffering kicks in.

6) tcpdump / wireshark approach to see where bytes are being held:
  sudo tcpdump -i lo -s 0 -w sse.pcap port 8080 or port 8083
  # then open pcap and watch timestamp of packets to detect where delays occur (server->nginx or nginx->client).

7) Repro variation: raw netcat server to eliminate Go runtime buffering:
  # start a manual server that writes with sleeps:
  while true; do \n    printf 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/event-stream\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n\r\n';
    for i in $(seq 1 10); do echo -n "$(printf '%x\r\n' 6)"; echo -n "data: $i\n\n"; sleep 1; done;
    echo -n "0\r\n\r\n";
  done | nc -l 8085

Hit through nginx proxy_pass to see if behavior is different. The goal is to see if plain tcp-level chunking is preserved.

Logs / error snippets seen: (copied)
  2026-02-20T15:12:04Z runtime: GC pause 120ms (allocation growth)
  2026-02-20T15:12:09Z nginx: [error] upstream prematurely closed connection while reading response header from upstream, client: 10.0.0.5, server: , request: "GET /sse/ HTTP/1.1", upstream: "http://127.0.0.1:8083/sse", host: "staging-api..."
  client logs: Fetch stream stalled, then resumed with ~3KB of buffered data.

Quick checklist of things tried and results:
- Turned off nginx proxy_buffering -> partial improvement (fewer big bursts)
- Added proxy_set_header Connection "" (remove 'upgrade' or 'close') -> no effect
- Verified Go server calls flusher.Flush() after each Write -> no change when hitting ALB in front (implies upstream LB buffering)
- Disabled gzip middleware -> slight improvement (makes sense, compression sometimes needs a buffer before emitting)
- Switched requests to HTTP/1.1 explicitly on client -> more consistent behavior (http2 seemed to coalesce frames)
- Reproduced using raw netcat -> showed streaming preserved; suggests runtime-level flush is possible, issue comes from real proxy/ALB in path

Action items / next steps: (for follow-up)
- Ask infra to check ALB / TLS termination config: are they buffering or applying any proxy buffers? Confirm idle timeout and max buffer sizes.
- Add X-Accel-Buffering: no (nginx) header from server side to force no buffering in any upstream reverse proxies that honor it.
- Add debug endpoint that returns each event with a sequence number + timestamp (server_ts + proxy_ts if possible) to identify where the delay occurs.
- Instrument server to log flush counts and bytes written (so we can correlate server writes with network packets).
- Re-run tcpdump on both sides (server->nginx and nginx->client) to pinpoint where bytes pause.
- If ALB buffering is unavoidable, consider using WebSocket or use chunked transfer + small flush-friendly writes (single byte flush) as a fallback for critical low-latency streams.

Quick reference commands to share in Slack when asking for help:
  # show headers and streaming behavior (verbose)
  curl -i -N -v --http1.1 http://localhost:8080/sse/ 2>&1 | sed -n '1,200p'
  # tcpdump capture (server and proxy)
  sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -s 0 -w /tmp/sse-server.pcap port 8083 &
  sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -s 0 -w /tmp/sse-proxy.pcap host <proxy-ip> &

Notes to self: HTTP streaming is fragile when many components (ALB, CDN, nginx, gzip) are in the path; each may buffer to optimize throughput. The most effective mitigations I found so far: disable buffering at proxy, disable compression for SSE endpoints, ensure server calls Flush(), and prefer HTTP/1.1 for simpler chunking semantics. But ALB-level buffering remains the likely cause for the staging intermittent pauses — need infra follow-up.

If I get more time: write a small harness that starts a local nginx + go server + optional HAProxy/ALB simulator and runs head-to-head curl loads while capturing pcaps. Would help us make a convincing report for infra/ops.

End of notes.
